lesson.title: Saturated and Unsaturated Fats: How a Single Double Bond Bends a Molecule
lesson.summary: Saturated fatty acids pack their carbon chains with the maximum possible number of hydrogens, while unsaturated fatty acids contain one or more carbon to carbon double bonds that kink the chain, and that geometric difference is the reason butter is solid while olive oil pours freely.
lesson.body:
The words saturated and unsaturated describe how many hydrogen atoms a fatty acid's carbon chain is carrying relative to the maximum it could hold. A saturated fatty acid has every available bonding position on its carbon backbone filled with a hydrogen atom, connected only by single covalent bonds between adjacent carbons. Because a single covalent bond involves one shared pair of electrons and allows free rotation around the bond axis, a saturated chain has no fixed kinks and can flex into a fully extended, essentially straight zigzag shape. An unsaturated fatty acid, by contrast, contains one or more carbon to carbon double bonds somewhere along the chain, meaning two carbons share two pairs of electrons rather than one, and each of those carbons has one fewer hydrogen attached than it would in a fully saturated chain, hence unsaturated.

That double bond matters mechanically as much as chemically. A single covalent bond allows the atoms on either side to rotate freely around it, but a double bond does not: the second shared electron pair locks the geometry in place, holding the atoms and substituents on either side in a fixed planar arrangement. In the double bonds found in natural unsaturated fatty acids, that fixed arrangement is almost always the cis configuration, meaning the hydrogen atoms on the two carbons of the double bond sit on the same side of the chain. That cis geometry forces a rigid kink into what would otherwise be a straight hydrocarbon tail, roughly a thirty degree bend at each double bond.

Those kinks change how the molecules pack together, and packing determines whether a fat is solid or liquid at room temperature. Saturated fatty acids, being straight, line up closely side by side, and the resulting tight packing allows relatively strong van der Waals interactions between neighboring chains, which raises the melting point enough that saturated fats like butter, lard, and coconut oil are solid at room temperature. Unsaturated fatty acids, with their kinked tails, cannot pack nearly as closely, weakening those same interactions and lowering the melting point, which is why unsaturated fats like olive oil, canola oil, and fish oil remain liquid at room temperature. Monounsaturated fats contain exactly one double bond, while polyunsaturated fats contain two or more, and each additional double bond adds another kink, generally lowering the melting point further.

One more variant is worth knowing because it does not occur naturally in significant amounts: trans fats. Industrial partial hydrogenation of vegetable oils, historically used to make oils more solid and shelf stable for products like margarine, can convert some natural cis double bonds into the trans configuration, where the two hydrogens on the double bonded carbons sit on opposite sides of the chain instead of the same side. A trans double bond does not introduce the same sharp kink a cis double bond does, so a trans unsaturated fatty acid behaves structurally more like a saturated one, packing tightly and raising melting point, while still technically containing a double bond.

The saturated versus unsaturated distinction is not just about physical state at room temperature, it carries forward directly into the next two sections. It determines how triglycerides made from these fatty acids behave, and it shapes how tightly or loosely a phospholipid bilayer's tails pack together, which in turn influences how fluid or rigid a cell membrane is.
